messages:
anya: Heads-up — hit ENI/IP exhaustion during a Karpenter trial in eu-west-1. One of the GPU provisioner attempts failed to launch additional nodes because the subnet reported no available IPs. Thinking this is a multi-AZ / vpc-cidr + CNI limit problem, not Karpenter itself. Anyone seen this pattern and have a game plan?

maria: yep, seen that. AWS CNI per-instance IP limits + small subnets bite you when you consolidate into fewer AZs.

tyler: can you paste the error from the Karpenter controller / events? usually it shows failed to bind because no capacity in subnet.

anya: pasted from controller: 

```
E1208 12:13:45.123456       1 provisioning.go:256] launch failed for Provisioner(gpu-prod-eu) : failed to create instance: InvalidParameterException: No more available private IPv4 addresses in subnet 'subnet-0a1b2c3d'
```

samir: yup that's the one. Two levers: increase subnet CIDR / add more subnets across AZs, or change provisioning to spread across AZs and instance types with higher ENI/IP capacity.

maria: for GPUs specifically we also worry about instance family availability per AZ. If you force topology spread without fallback, Karpenter will keep retrying and you'll have pending pods.

tyler: options we debated: (1) per-AZ provisioner CRs (one provisioner per subnet/AZ) so Karpenter can do localized decisions; (2) a global provisioner with subnetSelector and topology constraints; (3) hybrid: per-AZ provisioners but a lower-priority global fallback that can use other instance families or od/spot mix.

devex-engr: note that per-AZ provisioners complicate consolidation. Karpenter consolidation tries to terminate empty nodes to save cost; if provisioners are AZ-scoped you can still consolidate within AZ, but cross-AZ consolidation won't happen. Might increase fragmentation.

anya: good point. For cost we want consolidation, but for availability we want multi-AZ spread. tradeoffs.

samir: concrete pattern that worked at a few places:
- create 3 small subnets (one per AZ) with larger /20 CIDRs if possible
- create 3 provisioners, each with a subnetSelector limiting to an AZ-specific subnet (so Karpenter won't accidentally try to cram into a busy subnet)
- enable consolidation but add a policy to exclude GPU nodes (taint GPUs with "dedicated=gpupool:NoSchedule" for long-running training) so they don't get cycled aggressively
- a global fallback provisioner with broader instanceTypes and a different weight to prefer spare capacity for short-lived pods

anya: can you sketch an example provisioner we might use?

maria: sure — rough snippet for an AZ-scoped provisioner: 

```
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: provisioner-eu-west-1a-gpu
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      operator: In
      values: [eu-west-1a]
    - key: kubernetes.io/arch
      operator: In
      values: [amd64]
  provider:
    subnetSelector:
      Name: "redwood-eu-west-1a-gpu-subnet"
    instanceProfile: "redwood-node-profile"
  consolidation:
    enabled: true
  taints:
    - key: dedicated
      value: gpupool
      effect: NoSchedule
  limits:
    resources:
      cpu: "1000"
      memory: "2000Gi"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "200"
```

samir: couple other practical bits:
- set a graceful termination period on GPU workloads and use PodDisruptionBudgets to avoid killing active trainings during consolidation.
- prefer instance types with more ENIs/IPs (e.g., p4d has a decent ratio, and some C6gn-ish families) depending on AWS.
- monitor `kubectl get nodes -o wide` + `aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids` to map ENI usage when debugging.

tyler: also consider using the amazon-vpc-cni-custom networking config or secondary ENIs for high IP density if subnet resizing isn't an option. But that adds ops complexity and potential cross-account ipam headaches.

devex-engr: about cluster-autoscaler vs Karpenter — CA relies on ASGs and hits the same subnet/IP limits indirectly (if ASG launches instances into a saturated subnet they fail). Karpenter's approach is more flexible (it picks instance types + AZ) but still constrained by VPC IPs.

maria: for eu-west we hit sporadic AZ capacity for GPU spot. We introduced a fallback policy to auto-fall back to ondemand for critical job queues and keep a small reserved dedicated pool in a single AZ for guaranteed throughput. saves cost but keeps SLAs.

anya: can we add an alert in Console/Datadog for "subnet available ip < 20%" + tie it to provisioning failures so infra ops gets a page before apps pile up?

infra-bot: alert created: SUBNET_IP_LOW (eu-west-1a). Threshold: 15% available. PagerDuty: #infra-oncall. Link: https://datadog.example/incidents/RED-1234 :bell:

samir: also add a metric for Karpenter Provisioner launch failures (error counts / 5m) and a graph of recent instance type selection to spot overconcentration.

tyler: action items I see:
- expand subnet CIDR where possible (cloud team)
- create per-AZ provisioners + a global fallback (infra)
- mark GPU long-running pods with taint+PDB to avoid consolidation churn (platform)
- add Datadog alerts and Karpenter failure metric (sre)

anya: agree. I'll open a short RFC with the proposed YAML + rollout plan for canary in eu-west-1 (start in a test cluster, then prod). Will flag the reserved pool, and request cloud team to look at subnet sizing.

maria: one more note — document the subnet limits and preferred instance families in the ops runbook so oncall can triage fast.

anya: thanks all — I'll follow up with the RFC and link here when ready. :thumbsup:
